lines.text: English has an extraordinarily rich set of movement verbs, each conveying not just motion but manner, speed, and attitude. Walking alone branches into dozens of variations: you stroll through a park (leisurely), stride across a room (purposefully), trudge through mud (wearily), shuffle along a corridor (slowly, dragging feet), tiptoe past a sleeping child (quietly), and stomp up the stairs (angrily). Running has similar range: you sprint to catch a bus (fast, short burst), jog around the neighbourhood (steady exercise pace), dash to the shops (hurry briefly), and bolt from danger (flee suddenly). Climbing vocabulary includes scramble (climb awkwardly using hands and feet), clamber (climb with difficulty), and scale (climb something very high or steep). Jumping expands into leap (jump far or high with energy), hop (jump on one foot or small jumps), skip (step-hop alternating feet, playful), and bound (jump with large, energetic strides). Water movement gives us wade (walk through water), paddle (shallow playful water movement), and plunge (dive or fall suddenly into water). Each verb paints a different picture, and choosing the right one transforms flat prose into vivid narrative. A character doesn't just 'walk' — they saunter, limp, march, or creep, and each word tells you something about their mood, physical state, and intention.

lines.text: The British love walking. 'Going for a walk' is a national pastime, and the UK has over 140,000 miles of public footpaths. Terms like 'ramble', 'hike', 'trek', and 'stroll' distinguish different types: a ramble is leisurely countryside walking; a hike is more strenuous.

lines.text: English literature is famous for its precise movement verbs. Dickens' characters scurry, Tolkien's hobbits trudge, and Austen's heroines glide. Choosing the right verb is considered a mark of good writing — creative writing classes devote entire sessions to it.

lines.text: English movement is packed with phrasal verbs: 'set off' (begin a journey), 'head out' (leave), 'pop in' (visit briefly), 'swing by' (make a casual visit), 'nip out' (go out quickly). These are essential for natural-sounding English.
lines.name: English movement is packed with phrasal verbs: 'set off' (begin a journey), 'head out' (leave), 'pop in' (visit briefly), 'swing by' (make a casual visit), 'nip out' (go out quickly). These are essential for natural-sounding English.

lines.text: Many movement verbs come from sport: 'sprint' (athletics), 'dive' (swimming), 'tackle' (football/rugby), 'vault' (gymnastics). These cross into everyday language: 'I'll tackle that problem', 'She dived into the project'.

lines.text: The sport of parkour has introduced new movement vocabulary: 'vault' (jump over), 'wall run', 'precision jump', 'cat leap'. While niche, these terms appear in action films and video games, making them familiar to younger English speakers.

lines.text: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb — 'fastly' doesn't exist. 'He runs fast' (adverb). 'He is a fast runner' (adjective). Same applies to 'hard' — never 'hardly' (which means 'barely').

lines.text: 'Walk' is flat movement. For upward movement on mountains, use 'climb', 'hike', 'trek', or 'ascend'. 'Walk to the mountain' means approach it, not go up it.
